title: POC scoping: Quality eval & load benchmarks - AstraNovus
summary: Kickoff scoping for a 4-week POC focused on quality evaluation and load benchmarking. Agreed success criteria: <15% hallucination by automatic checks + human spot-check pass rate >= 90% on golden prompts, end-to-end latency p95 < 900ms for typical 2k token request mix, and sustained throughput of 220 rps at tail under dedicated config. Plan: generate golden prompts, run regression suite, run hallucination/format checks, draft scoring rubric, run 3-phase benchmark (dev, canary, full), Redwood to provide config recommendations and estimate GPU units. Next: Redwood to send eval templates, security docs, and pricing for dedicated pool; customer to share sample prompt set and 500 de-identified examples.
next_steps: Redwood: send golden-prompt template and eval spreadsheet by 2026-02-18
Customer: share 500 de-identified examples and current inference logs by 2026-02-20
Schedule lab benchmark window week of 2026-02-23
action_items: Mike Alvarez - Send eval template, benchmarks spreadsheet, and security brief - 2026-02-18
Priya Desai - Draft initial scoring rubric and hallucination detection pipeline notes - 2026-02-17
Dr. Serena Koh - Deliver 500 de-identified examples and list of priority intents - 2026-02-20
Ethan Morris - Confirm network/VPC constraints and expected SLA for production - 2026-02-19
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-02-15 16:00 UTC | Duration 52m | Attendees: Mike (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Jordan (SA), Dr. Serena (AstraNovus Head of ML), Ethan (CTO), Laura (Platform), Samir (Data)

[00:00] Mike: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, really quick roll call - we have Priya and Jordan from our side, and Serena, Ethan, Laura, Samir with AstraNovus, right?
[00:12] Dr. Serena: Yep that's right. Thanks for doing this, we've been excited to scope this.
[00:18] Priya: Awesome. The goal for today is to lock success criteria for the POC and agree on the quality evaluation plan plus how we'll size the load and benchmarks. We'll also outline timelines.
[00:30] Ethan: Great. To give a quick context we currently run a mix of open models in prod via an internal kube-based stack and some SageMaker endpoints for heavy jobs. We're trying to standardize inference and reduce cost while improving factuality for our clinical summarization feature.
[00:45] Jordan: When you say clinical summarization, are you doing single-document summarization or multi-doc? Typical lengths?
[00:53] Dr. Serena: Mostly multi-doc. Average request size is around 1.6k tokens, peak up to 3k when we collate several notes. Throughput-wise we see bursts up to ~200 req/min during ingest windows.
[01:06] Mike: Okay that helps a lot. For the POC we recommend a representative sample: 500 de-identified examples across short, medium, long flows so we can create golden prompts and regression cases.
[01:18] Samir: We can provide those, yes. One ask — we need to ensure nothing leaves our VPC in identifiable form, that the audit logs are captured. SOC 2 is a must.
[01:30] Priya: Understood. We'll include the SOC 2 and encryption/KMS notes. Note, our private deployment option will keep data in your VPC if needed.
[01:41] Ethan: For success criteria, we're thinking of two axes: quality (factuality/hallucination + format correctness) and performance (latency/throughput/cost). Can we enumerate concrete thresholds?
[01:54] Mike: Sure. From similar POCs we typically see customers land on something like: automated hallucination checks under 15% false-positive rate and human spot-check pass rate >= 90% on golden prompts. For latency: end-to-end p95 under 900ms for your 2k token mix on a dedicated configuration, and sustained throughput 200-250 rps depending on batching. Cost target we can estimate after model choice and quantization.
[02:18] Dr. Serena: The 15% hallucination number — how do you measure that automatically?
[02:23] Priya: Good question. We use a hybrid approach: automated NLI-style checks + knowledge-based heuristics for clinical entities, plus a human review sample. Basically auto-check flags likely hallucinations, we then compute a precision/recall estimate against human labels in the sample. The POC will calibrate that.
[02:40] Laura: On format correctness, our product expects a strict JSON schema for the output. If it wanders, downstream parsers fail.
[02:48] Jordan: So we'll add schema enforcement tests: sample prompts with expected JSON outputs, and a short harness to run structural checks and measure percent of outputs that validate.
[02:58] Ethan: Timeline wise we prefer a four-week POC: week 1 ingest & golden prompt alignment, week 2 run regression & small dev benchmarks, week 3 canary larger benchmarks, week 4 final analysis and handoff. Is that realistic?
[03:12] Mike: Yes that's our recommended cadence. We'll need the sample data by Feb 20 to meet that.
[03:20] Dr. Serena: About golden prompts — we'd like Redwood to help craft them. What does a golden prompt look like for you?
[03:26] Priya: We usually create 20-30 golden prompts covering happy path, edge cases, and adversarial examples. Each golden prompt includes: the input set, the expected output (or verification rules), and a difficulty label. Example: "Summarize these three visit notes into a JSON with keys diagnosis[], meds[], and plan[] — do not hallucinate new diagnoses."
[03:44] Samir: Can you share an example template?
[03:46] Mike: We'll send a template; action item.
[03:49] [03:49] Mike: Also, for hallucination detection, sometimes semantic checks alone miss subtle hallucinations. We recommend adding a reference-check step where outputs are cross-checked against the source docs or a retrieval augmentation hit. If retrieval score is low, flag for human review.
[04:05] Dr. Serena: We already have retrieval annotated in some cases; we can provide the pipeline connectors.
[04:10] Priya: Perfect. For scoring approach: hybrid metric. Automated scores include schema-validate %, hallucination flags per automated model, and a token-level overlap metric for certain structured fields. Human eval will be a 3-point rubric (correct / partially correct / incorrect) for factuality and a binary for format. We'll compute weighted score; suggest quality threshold >= 0.9 for POC success.
[04:33] Ethan: How do we handle regression tests? We need to ensure new model rollouts don't regress on key intents.
[04:38] Jordan: We'll set up a regression harness where golden prompts + a larger set of N examples (we recommend 2k) are run nightly in the POC. Any drop > 3% in the weighted quality score triggers alerts. For the POC we do daytime runs to conserve budget.
[04:53] Laura: Network constraints — in production we have a tight egress policy, can Redwood work in a private deployment in our VPC?
[04:59] Mike: Yes, Redwood Private supports control plane outside and inference inside your VPC, or fully managed on-prem for stricter environments. We'll bless the options and include SSO/SAML notes, though please forgive if auto transcribed SAML becomes Samuel in the doc.
[05:14] Dr. Serena: (laughs) good to note.
[05:17] Ethan: For benchmarks, can we see p50/p95 token latencies per model variant and cost per 1M tokens?
[05:23] Priya: Absolutely. We'll propose a bench matrix: models (open-llama-like, mid-size LLM, Redwood-verified variants), sequence lengths (512, 1.6k, 3k), batching profiles, and quantization (fp16 vs 8-bit). Output: p50/p95 latency, tokens/sec per GPU, and estimated dollar cost per 1M tokens.
[05:47] Samir: What's realistic GPU sizing for our peak?
[05:50] Jordan: Rough ballpark — for a medium 13B-equivalent model with batching tuned you might need 1 GPU per 500-800 concurrent active sessions depending on KV cache hit rate. We'll firm this up once we see your real usage traces.
[06:03] Dr. Serena: KV cache — we have lots of reuse across prompts; caching is important. Please don't call it KV cash in the doc.
[06:09] Mike: Noted, KV cache.
[06:11] [06:11] Priya: A couple of gotchas we usually highlight: 1) hallucination metrics are sensitive to how you sample human labels; 2) format validation can be brittle if prompts don't anchor the model, so we recommend explicit function-calling or JSON instructions and a post-processor that enforces schema.
[06:28] Ethan: For the human review portion, can Redwood provide tooling to label outputs?
[06:32] Mike: We can provide a lightweight labeling view in the console or a CSV template for internal labeling, whichever you prefer.
[06:40] Dr. Serena: On scoring weights, we want to emphasize factuality over format — maybe 0.6 factuality, 0.3 format, 0.1 latency/cost. Is that configurable?
[06:50] Priya: Yes, totally. We'll ship a default weighting but the rubric will be editable.
[06:55] Jordan: For automation, we'll also include a regression threshold for each intent. Some intents are safety-critical and have a 0% tolerance for hallucination.
[07:05] Samir: Safety-critical intents — how do we surface them?
[07:08] Dr. Serena: We'll provide a list of 10 priority intents to be treated as high-risk.
[07:13] Mike: Good. Now on deliverables: Redwood will provide: 1) golden prompt template + initial 30 prompts, 2) eval spreadsheet + scoring rubric, 3) benchmark plan and required infra (GPU estimate), 4) security brief (SOC2/KMS/SSO notes). AstraNovus to provide: 500 examples + logs + list of high-risk intents + VPC constraints.
[07:36] Ethan: Pricing — will we get a rough estimate for dedicated pool for the POC?
[07:40] Mike: We'll include a POC pricing estimate and an optional dedicated reserved estimate. Note that quantization and batching can materially change cost.
[07:48] Dr. Serena: One other thing: hallucination definition — is generation of unsupported diagnoses always a hall? There is nuance sometimes model will infer plausible but not present items.
[07:58] Priya: Correct, that's why human labeling is important. In the automated pipeline we flag entities that are not matched to source text as potential hallucinations; then humans adjudicate. For the POC we capture both the automated rate and human-adjusted precision.
[08:13] Mike: Any blockers on data sharing?
[08:16] Samir: We need a DPA and assurance that the de-id process matches our legal standards. We'll get legal to sign DPA but in parallel we'll share de-identified samples.
[08:26] Mike: Sounds fair. We'll send the DPA template and security docs with the action items.
[08:30] [08:30] Priya: Quick note on monitoring during the benchmark: we'll enable token-level cost breakdown, per-route latency, and per-prompt quality tagging so we can correlate quality dips to traffic patterns.
[08:44] Ethan: Excellent. Anything else on the evaluation methodology?
[08:47] Dr. Serena: For regression tests, please include adversarial prompts — we have a few examples where models hallucinate heavily. We'll contribute those.
[08:55] Priya: We'll add adversarial set and calibrate scoring to penalize hallucination more heavily there.
[09:01] Jordan: Final recap then: deliverables and dates captured in action items; schedule bench week of Feb 23; Redwood sends templates by Feb 18; AstraNovus sends samples by Feb 20.
[09:15] Mike: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with a short email summarizing these notes and attaching the decks.
[09:21] Dr. Serena: Thanks all. Looking forward to it.
[09:25] Mike: Bye.

Transcript notes: occasional transcription errors present (SAML -> Samuel, KV cache sometimes transcribed as KV cash), speaker overlaps minimal.
